claim: PV+ interneurons constitute less than 2% of the total neuronal population in the hippocampus.
source: Parvalbumin (PV+) interneurons constitute a small proportion of the total neuronal population (less than 2% in the hippocampus), yet they possess crucial roles in shaping neuronal network activity (Freund and Buzsáki, 1996; Jonas et al., 2004; Pelkey et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Freund and Buzsáki, 1996; Jonas et al., 2004; Pelkey et al., 2017).

claim: PV+ interneurons have crucial roles in shaping neuronal network activity.
source: Parvalbumin (PV+) interneurons constitute a small proportion of the total neuronal population (less than 2% in the hippocampus), yet they possess crucial roles in shaping neuronal network activity (Freund and Buzsáki, 1996; Jonas et al., 2004; Pelkey et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Freund and Buzsáki, 1996; Jonas et al., 2004; Pelkey et al., 2017).

claim: PV+ interneurons inhibit their postsynaptic targets efficiently by applying fast perisomatic inhibition.
source: PV+ interneurons inhibit their postsynaptic targets efficiently by applying fast perisomatic inhibition and have been directly implicated in the generation of network activity at the gamma (γ) band frequency (30–80 Hz) (Antonoudiou et al., 2020; Cardin et al., 2009; Hájos et al., 2004; Mann et al., 2005; Sohal et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Antonoudiou et al., 2020; Cardin et al., 2009; Hájos et al., 2004; Mann et al., 2005; Sohal et al., 2009).

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Antonoudiou et al., 2020; Cardin et al., 2009; Hájos et al., 2004; Mann et al., 2005; Sohal et al., 2009).

claim: Network oscillations at γ-band frequency are believed to facilitate information transmission through circuit synchronization and local gain control.
source: Network oscillations at γ-band frequency are believed to facilitate information transmission through circuit synchronization and local gain control that may be instrumental in multiple cognitive processes such as attention, learning, and memory (Akam and Kullmann, 2010; Fries, 2015; Howard et al., 2003; Montgomery and Buzsaki, 2007; Sohal, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Akam and Kullmann, 2010; Fries, 2015; Howard et al., 2003; Montgomery and Buzsaki, 2007; Sohal, 2016).

claim: γ-band oscillations may be instrumental in multiple cognitive processes such as attention, learning, and memory.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Akam and Kullmann, 2010; Fries, 2015; Howard et al., 2003; Montgomery and Buzsaki, 2007; Sohal, 2016).

claim: γ-band oscillations are thought to be metabolically very costly.
source: Importantly, these oscillations are thought to be metabolically very costly, and it has therefore been postulated that PV+ interneurons require substantial amounts of energy via ATP hydrolysis to sustain the high firing rate and dissipate ion gradients during neuronal transmission (Attwell and Laughlin, 2001; Kann, 2011; Kann, 2016; Kann and Kovács, 2007; Kann et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Attwell and Laughlin, 2001; Kann, 2011; Kann, 2016; Kann and Kovács, 2007; Kann et al., 2014).

claim: PV+ interneurons have a higher density of energy-producing mitochondria.
source: Indeed, electron microscopy, histochemical, and transcriptomic approaches have revealed that PV+ interneurons have a higher density of energy-producing mitochondria and elevated expression levels of electron transport chain components (Adams et al., 2015; Gulyás et al., 2006; Nie and Wong-Riley, 1995; Paul et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Adams et al., 2015; Gulyás et al., 2006; Nie and Wong-Riley, 1995; Paul et al., 2017).

claim: The spatiotemporal organization of mitochondria is essential for the precise provision of ATP and Ca2+-buffering for neuronal transmission and communication.

claim: Miro1 is a mitochondrial adaptor protein, responsible for coupling mitochondria to the cytoskeleton and for their bidirectional trafficking in axons and dendrites.
source: Miro1 is a mitochondrial adaptor protein, responsible for coupling mitochondria to the cytoskeleton and for their bidirectional trafficking in axons and dendrites (Birsa et al., 2013; Guo et al., 2005; López-Doménech et al., 2016; López-Doménech et al., 2018; Macaskill et al., 2009; Nguyen et al., 2014; Saotome et al., 2008; Wang and Schwarz, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Birsa et al., 2013; Guo et al., 2005; López-Doménech et al., 2016; López-Doménech et al., 2018; Macaskill et al., 2009; Nguyen et al., 2014; Saotome et al., 2008; Wang and Schwarz, 2009).

claim: Global deletion of Miro1 (encoded by the Rhot1 gene) is perinatal lethal.
source: Global deletion of Miro1 (encoded by the Rhot1 gene) is perinatal lethal, while the conditional removal of Miro1 from cortical and hippocampal pyramidal cells alters the occupancy of dendritic mitochondria due to impairment in trafficking, resulting in dendritic degeneration and cell death (López-Doménech et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (López-Doménech et al., 2016).

claim: Conditional removal of Miro1 from cortical and hippocampal pyramidal cells alters the occupancy of dendritic mitochondria due to impairment in trafficking, resulting in dendritic degeneration and cell death.
source: Global deletion of Miro1 (encoded by the Rhot1 gene) is perinatal lethal, while the conditional removal of Miro1 from cortical and hippocampal pyramidal cells alters the occupancy of dendritic mitochondria due to impairment in trafficking, resulting in dendritic degeneration and cell death (López-Doménech et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (López-Doménech et al., 2016).

claim: The cumulative length of PV+ interneuron axon reaches up to 50 mm in the hippocampus.
source: In contrast, the significance of mitochondrial trafficking and distribution in PV+ interneurons, and the role of Miro1, is completely unexplored and especially interesting as their axon is highly branched with a cumulative length reaching up to 50 mm in the hippocampus (Hu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Hu et al., 2014).

claim: The protein levels of COX-IV were elevated in PV immuno-positive regions (3.6 × 10−6 ± 1.33 × 10−5 a.u.) when compared to immuno-negative areas in hippocampal slices (2.8 × 10−6 ± 1.26 × 10−5 a.u., p<0.0001, Mann–Whitney U test).
source: Consistent with this finding, we also observed that the protein levels of subunit IV of cytochrome c oxidase (COX-IV) were elevated in PV immuno-positive regions (3.6 × 10−6 ± 1.33 × 10−5 a.u.) when compared to immuno-negative areas in hippocampal slices (2.8 × 10−6 ± 1.26 × 10−5 a.u., Figure 1A, p<0.0001, Mann–Whitney U test), further supporting that PV+ interneurons rely heavily on mitochondria.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1A and statistical analysis (Mann-Whitney U test, p<0.0001).

claim: The number of MitoDendra-expressing PV+ cells did not vary in the hippocampus of control (Miro1 WT), hemi-floxed (Miro1 HET), and conditional knock-out (Miro1 KO) animals.
source: Indeed, the number of MitoDendra-expressing PV+ cells did not vary in the hippocampus of control (Miro1 WT: PvalbCre Rhot1+/+), hemi-floxed (Miro1 HET: PvalbCre Rhot1flox/+), and conditional knock-out (Miro1 KO: PvalbCre Rhot1flox/flox) animals (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The Miro1 fluorescence intensity was significantly reduced in PV+ interneurons from brain slices of knock-out mice (HET 844 ± 32.8 a.u., KO 518 ± 20.5 a.u., p<0.0001, Mann–Whitney U test).

evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and statistical analysis (Mann-Whitney U test, p<0.0001).

claim: There was a significant reduction in the percentage of moving mitochondria in the absence of Miro1 when compared to the control (WT 23 ± 3%, ΗΕT 21 ± 2%, KO 9 ± 3%, pKO = 0.002).

evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1C and statistical analysis (Tukey's multiple comparisons test, ordinary one-way ANOVA, pKO = 0.002).

claim: There was an enhancement in axonal branching in the proximal axon (between 50 μm and 200 μm from the cell body) when Miro1 was knocked-out.

claim: The amplitude of sEPSCs was elevated in Miro1 KO (−188 ± 17.2 pA) slices when compared to control slices (−130 ± 7.8 pA, p = 0.009, unpaired t-test with Welch's correction).

evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: No robust difference was observed in spatial exploration of WT and Miro1 KO animals in the open-field assessment.
source: We also did not observe a robust difference in spatial exploration of WT and Miro1 KO animals in the open-field assessment (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D; Seibenhener and Wooten, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The velocity, distance traveled, and time spent in the areas of the arena were not statistically different between WT and Miro1 KO genotypes.
source: The velocity (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E), distance traveled (Figure 5—figure supplement 2F), and time spent in the areas of the arena (Figure 5—figure supplement 2G) were not statistically different between the two genotypes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 2E, 2F, and 2G.

claim: The Miro1 KO animals spent more time in the open arms (18 ± 5%) than their littermate controls (6 ± 1%, p = 0.004, Mann–Whitney U test).
source: The Miro1 KO animals however spent more time in the open arms (18 ± 5%) than their littermate controls (6 ± 1%, Figure 5K, p = 0.004, Mann–Whitney U test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5K and statistical analysis (Mann-Whitney U test, p = 0.004).

claim: The performance of Miro1 KO animals in the EPM suggests that they may exhibit a reduced anxiety-like phenotype.
source: The performance of Miro1 KO animals in the EPM suggests that they may exhibit a reduced anxiety-like phenotype.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the behavioral data in the elevated plus maze.

claim: PV+ interneurons display increased levels of complex I, cytochrome c oxidase, cytochrome c, and ATP synthase.
source: This is consistent with evidence proposing high levels of oxidative phosphorylation proteins such as complex I, cytochrome c oxidase, cytochrome c, and ATP synthase in these cells (Gulyás et al., 2006; Kann et al., 2011; Paul et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Gulyás et al., 2006; Kann et al., 2011; Paul et al., 2017).

claim: PV+ interneurons are metabolically more active to meet their high-energy demands.
source: This observation could further support the notion that PV+ interneurons are metabolically more active to meet their high-energy demands and suggests that stringent dependence on mitochondrial function could render PV+ interneurons susceptible to incidents of mitochondrial damage.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of high levels of oxidative phosphorylation proteins in PV+ interneurons.

claim: Stringent dependence on mitochondrial function could render PV+ interneurons susceptible to incidents of mitochondrial damage.
source: This observation could further support the notion that PV+ interneurons are metabolically more active to meet their high-energy demands and suggests that stringent dependence on mitochondrial function could render PV+ interneurons susceptible to incidents of mitochondrial damage.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the inference that high metabolic activity and dependence on mitochondria may increase vulnerability.

claim: Gene expression under the PV+ promoter begins around postnatal day 10 (P10) and is stabilized around P28.
source: Gene expression under the PV+ promoter begins around postnatal day 10 (P10) and is stabilized around P28 (Barnes et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Barnes et al., 2015).

claim: Cre-dependent removal of Miro1 is not expected to impact on the migration, differentiation, and viability of PV+ neurons.
source: Thus, Cre-dependent removal of Miro1 is not expected to impact on the migration, differentiation, and viability of PV+ neurons (Okaty et al., 2009; del Río et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Okaty et al., 2009; del Río et al., 1994).

claim: A small subset of mitochondria remained mobile in the absence of Miro1, indicating that mitochondrial transport was not completely abolished in Miro1 KO.
source: A small subset of mitochondria remained mobile in the absence of Miro1, indicating that mitochondrial transport was not completely abolished in Miro1 KO.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that some mitochondria still moved in Miro1 KO conditions.

claim: Other studies also report a reduction, but not complete cessation of mitochondrial transport, upon Miro1 loss.
source: Other studies also report a reduction, but not complete cessation of mitochondrial transport, upon Miro1 loss (López-Doménech et al., 2016; Macaskill et al., 2009; Russo et al., 2009), hinting to the existence of alternative mitochondrial transport mechanisms.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (López-Doménech et al., 2016; Macaskill et al., 2009; Russo et al., 2009).

claim: The physical attachment of mitochondria to other motor–adaptor proteins might still facilitate organelle transport.
source: The physical attachment of mitochondria to other motor–adaptor proteins might still facilitate organelle transport.
evidence: This claim is speculative, suggesting a possible mechanism for residual mitochondrial transport in the absence of Miro1.

claim: Trak1/2 motors can still be recruited to the mitochondria in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs), in a Miro1-independent fashion.
source: Our lab has demonstrated that Trak1/2 motors can still be recruited to the mitochondria in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs), in a Miro1-independent fashion (López-Doménech et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (López-Doménech et al., 2018).

claim: It is possible that the remaining moving mitochondria engaged with cytoskeletal elements other than microtubules.
source: Thus, it is also possible that the remaining moving mitochondria engaged with cytoskeletal elements other than microtubules.
evidence: This claim is speculative, suggesting a possible explanation for residual mitochondrial movement.

claim: Involvement of the actin cytoskeleton has been implicated in short-range mitochondrial movement.
source: Indeed, involvement of the actin cytoskeleton has been implicated in short-range mitochondrial movement (Chada and Hollenbeck, 2004; Morris and Hollenbeck, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Chada and Hollenbeck, 2004; Morris and Hollenbeck, 1995).

claim: The remaining moving mitochondria in the Miro1 KO model exhibited directional, rather than random movement, which favors transport along microtubules.
source: Still, the remaining moving mitochondria in our model exhibited directional, rather than random movement, which favors transport along microtubules.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation of directional movement of mitochondria.

claim: Similar perinuclear clustering has been reported upon the loss of Miro1 in MEFs and in the Camk2aCre Rhot1flox/flox mouse at 4 months of age.
source: Similar perinuclear clustering has also been reported upon the loss of Miro1 in MEFs (López-Doménech et al., 2018; Nguyen et al., 2014) and in the Camk2aCre Rhot1flox/flox mouse at 4 months of age (López-Doménech et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (López-Doménech et al., 2018; Nguyen et al., 2014; López-Doménech et al., 2016).

claim: Mutations in dMiro, the Drosophila orthologue, impair mitochondrial trafficking and deplete mitochondria from the axon, altering the morphology of both the axon and synaptic boutons in the neuromuscular junction.
source: Mutations in dMiro, the Drosophila orthologue, impair mitochondrial trafficking and deplete mitochondria from the axon, altering the morphology of both the axon and synaptic boutons in the neuromuscular junction (Guo et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Guo et al., 2005).

claim: Miro1 mediates the activity-dependent repositioning of mitochondria to synapses in excitatory neurons.
source: Miro1 also mediates the activity-dependent repositioning of mitochondria to synapses in excitatory neurons (Vaccaro et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Vaccaro et al., 2017).

claim: The loss of mitochondria from axonal terminals in Miro1 KO cells could be the consequence of defective protein-protein interactions with the tethering machinery, resulting in the inability of mitochondria to be retained in the presynaptic space.
source: We speculate that the loss of mitochondria from axonal terminals in Miro1 KO cells could be the consequence of defective protein-protein interactions with the tethering machinery, resulting in the inability of mitochondria to be retained in the presynaptic space.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a possible mechanism for mitochondrial depletion from axonal terminals.

claim: Mitochondrial transport on actin filaments mediates local distribution along the axon and destabilization of F-actin reduces mitochondrial docking.
source: Mitochondrial transport on actin filaments mediates local distribution along the axon and destabilization of F-actin reduces mitochondrial docking (Chada and Hollenbeck, 2003; Chada and Hollenbeck, 2004; Hirokawa et al., 2010; Shlevkov et al., 2019; Smith and Gallo, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Chada and Hollenbeck, 2003; Chada and Hollenbeck, 2004; Hirokawa et al., 2010; Shlevkov et al., 2019; Smith and Gallo, 2018).

claim: It is possible that the loss of Miro1 might have disrupted the interaction between mitochondria and the actin cytoskeleton resulting in reduced presynaptic capture due to impairments in the Myo19-dependent coupling to actin in the absence of Miro1.
source: It is therefore possible that the loss of Miro1 might have disrupted the interaction between mitochondria and the actin cytoskeleton resulting in reduced presynaptic capture for example due to impairments in the Myo19-dependent coupling to actin in the absence of Miro1 (López-Doménech et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a possible mechanism for reduced presynaptic mitochondrial capture, with support from a citation (López-Doménech et al., 2018).

claim: Neuronal mitochondrial misplacement is thought to impact on neuronal morphology as mitochondria are no longer precisely located in places where they are actively required to provide energy and buffer Ca2+.
source: Neuronal mitochondrial misplacement is thought to impact on neuronal morphology as mitochondria are no longer precisely located in places where they are actively required to provide energy and buffer Ca2+ (Devine and Kittler, 2018; Guo et al., 2005; Liu and Shio, 2008; López-Doménech et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Devine and Kittler, 2018; Guo et al., 2005; Liu and Shio, 2008; López-Doménech et al., 2016).

claim: The enhancement in axonal branching could be attributed to the perturbed mitochondrial distribution.
source: Since mitochondria were found closer to sites of branch points in the absence of Miro1, our data suggest that the enhancement in axonal branching could be attributed to the perturbed mitochondrial distribution (Figure 3I).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that mitochondria are closer to branch points in Miro1 KO.

claim: Mitochondrial arrest and presynaptic capture is necessary for axon extension and branching formation, as mitochondria can locally provide energy.
source: Mitochondrial arrest and presynaptic capture is necessary for axon extension and branching formation, as mitochondria can locally provide energy (Courchet et al., 2013; Sainath et al., 2017; Smith and Gallo, 2018; Spillane et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Courchet et al., 2013; Sainath et al., 2017; Smith and Gallo, 2018; Spillane et al., 2013).

claim: The extension and retraction of the axon are developmentally dynamic processes.
source: The extension and retraction of the axon are developmentally dynamic processes (Chattopadhyaya et al., 2004; Chattopadhyaya et al., 2007; Huang et al., 2007) and the Miro1-dependent changes in mitochondrial distribution could promote either the formation of branches close to the cell body or the reorganization of existing branches.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Chattopadhyaya et al., 2004; Chattopadhyaya et al., 2007; Huang et al., 2007).

claim: The Miro1-dependent changes in mitochondrial distribution could promote either the formation of branches close to the cell body or the reorganization of existing branches.
source: The extension and retraction of the axon are developmentally dynamic processes (Chattopadhyaya et al., 2004; Chattopadhyaya et al., 2007; Huang et al., 2007) and the Miro1-dependent changes in mitochondrial distribution could promote either the formation of branches close to the cell body or the reorganization of existing branches.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing possible mechanisms for the observed changes in axonal branching.

claim: PV+ interneurons are critical elements in generating and maintaining γ-oscillations.
source: PV+ interneurons are critical elements in generating and maintaining γ-oscillations (Antonoudiou et al., 2020; Bartos et al., 2007; Buzsáki and Wang, 2012; Cardin et al., 2009; Sohal et al., 2009), and these oscillations heavily rely on intact mitochondrial function (Galow et al., 2014; Huchzermeyer et al., 2008; Huchzermeyer et al., 2013; Kann et al., 2011; Kann et al., 2016; Whittaker et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Antonoudiou et al., 2020; Bartos et al., 2007; Buzsáki and Wang, 2012; Cardin et al., 2009; Sohal et al., 2009).

claim: γ-oscillations heavily rely on intact mitochondrial function.
source: PV+ interneurons are critical elements in generating and maintaining γ-oscillations (Antonoudiou et al., 2020; Bartos et al., 2007; Buzsáki and Wang, 2012; Cardin et al., 2009; Sohal et al., 2009), and these oscillations heavily rely on intact mitochondrial function (Galow et al., 2014; Huchzermeyer et al., 2008; Huchzermeyer et al., 2013; Kann et al., 2011; Kann et al., 2016; Whittaker et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Galow et al., 2014; Huchzermeyer et al., 2008; Huchzermeyer et al., 2013; Kann et al., 2011; Kann et al., 2016; Whittaker et al., 2011).

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of complex I with rotenone, and uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation with FCCP abolishes the power of γ-oscillations.
source: Indeed, pharmacological inhibition of complex I with rotenone, and uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation with FCCP abolishes the power of γ-oscillations (Whittaker et al., 2011), while rotenone also reduced oxygen consumption in the CA3 area of the hippocampus, coupling respiration to network activity (Kann et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Whittaker et al., 2011).

claim: Rotenone reduced oxygen consumption in the CA3 area of the hippocampus, coupling respiration to network activity.
source: Indeed, pharmacological inhibition of complex I with rotenone, and uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation with FCCP abolishes the power of γ-oscillations (Whittaker et al., 2011), while rotenone also reduced oxygen consumption in the CA3 area of the hippocampus, coupling respiration to network activity (Kann et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Kann et al., 2011).

claim: In addition to the proper functioning of mitochondria, their precise positioning along the axon might be important in the fine tuning of rhythmic oscillations in γ-frequency band.
source: These results suggest that in addition to the proper functioning of mitochondria, their precise positioning along the axon might be important in the fine tuning of rhythmic oscillations in γ-frequency band.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that loss of Miro1 affects γ-oscillation frequency.

claim: The Miro1-directed changes in mitochondrial dynamics were not sufficient to compromise PV+ interneuron output.
source: Surprisingly, the Miro1-directed changes in mitochondrial dynamics were not sufficient to compromise PV+ interneuron output (Figure 4), which would be directly reflected on the generation and maintenance of γ-oscillations in the hippocampus.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that PV+ interneuron-mediated inhibition remained intact despite changes in mitochondrial dynamics.

claim: Alterations in axonal branching could have an implication on the innervation of postsynaptic targets.
source: Alterations in axonal branching could have an implication on the innervation of postsynaptic targets (Huang et al., 2007), and it is therefore possible that the precise PV+ interneuron innervation of pyramidal cells changed (Figure 3H), resulting in an increase in the excitation PV+ interneurons received in the hippocampus (Figure 5A,B), without compromising inhibition (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Huang et al., 2007) and inference from the data.

claim: It is possible that the precise PV+ interneuron innervation of pyramidal cells changed, resulting in an increase in the excitation PV+ interneurons received in the hippocampus, without compromising inhibition.
source: Alterations in axonal branching could have an implication on the innervation of postsynaptic targets (Huang et al., 2007), and it is therefore possible that the precise PV+ interneuron innervation of pyramidal cells changed (Figure 3H), resulting in an increase in the excitation PV+ interneurons received in the hippocampus (Figure 5A,B), without compromising inhibition (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a possible mechanism for the observed changes in excitation.

claim: The extent of the axon reach in the hippocampus might be reduced resulting in each PV+ interneuron inhibiting a different number of postsynaptic cells in the local network, introducing variability in the synchronization of cell assemblies and an overall enhancement in the excitatory tone in the hippocampus.
source: We speculate that the extent of the axon reach in the hippocampus might be reduced resulting in each PV+ interneuron inhibiting a different number of postsynaptic cells in the local network, introducing variability in the synchronization of cell assemblies and an overall enhancement in the excitatory tone in the hippocampus (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a possible mechanism for the observed changes in network activity.

claim: Neuronal entrainment at γ-frequencies during development can impact neuronal morphology of cortical cells.
source: Furthermore, recent work proposed that neuronal entrainment at γ-frequencies during development can impact neuronal morphology of cortical cells (Bitzenhofer et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Bitzenhofer et al., 2019).

claim: The changes in mitochondrial distribution associated with the impairments in Miro1-directed trafficking are not sufficient to alter the perisomatic inhibition applied by PV+ interneurons.
source: Surprisingly, given the established role of mitochondria in presynaptic release (Devine and Kittler, 2018; Sun et al., 2013), neither spontaneous inhibitory postsynaptic transmission nor PV+ interneuron-mediated evoked inhibition was altered by the reduction of mitochondria in axonal boutons in Miro1 KO (Figure 4), demonstrating that the changes in mitochondrial distribution associated with the impairments in Miro1-directed trafficking are not sufficient to alter the perisomatic inhibition applied by PV+ interneurons.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that inhibition remained intact despite mitochondrial depletion from boutons.

claim: The Ca2+ buffering capabilities of the parvalbumin protein might compensate for the absence of the local mitochondrial pool and participate in synaptic release by sequestering Ca2+.
source: The Ca2+ buffering capabilities of the parvalbumin protein might compensate for the absence of the local mitochondrial pool and participate in synaptic release by sequestering Ca2+.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a possible compensatory mechanism.

claim: Genetic removal of the parvalbumin protein has an impact on inhibitory transmission, synaptic facilitation, and network activity.
source: Genetic removal of the parvalbumin protein has an impact on inhibitory transmission, synaptic facilitation, and network activity (Caillard et al., 2000; Eggermann and Jonas, 2011; Orduz et al., 2013; Vreugdenhil et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Caillard et al., 2000; Eggermann and Jonas, 2011; Orduz et al., 2013; Vreugdenhil et al., 2003).

claim: Ca2+ signaling in PV+ interneurons may be modulated by the interplay of various buffers such as mitochondria and parvalbumin itself.
source: Thus, Ca2+ signaling in PV+ interneurons may be modulated by the interplay of various buffers such as mitochondria and parvalbumin itself.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that inhibition is maintained despite mitochondrial depletion.

claim: The increased cellular concentration of mitochondria in PV+ interneurons ensures sufficient metabolic capacity to support their energetic demands.
source: It is also possible that the increased cellular concentration of mitochondria in PV+ interneurons ensures sufficient metabolic capacity to support their energetic demands.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a possible explanation for maintained function despite mitochondrial redistribution.

claim: Local ATP synthesis and provision is required during sustained synaptic activity.
source: Although reports have shown the requirement of local ATP synthesis and provision during sustained synaptic activity (Rangaraju et al., 2014; Sun et al., 2013), which is facilitated via the Ca2+ uptake by mitochondria (Ashrafi et al., 2020), the diffusion of ATP from mitochondria rich regions to boutons devoid of mitochondria may be sufficient to sustain the energetic requirements of synapses (Pathak et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Rangaraju et al., 2014; Sun et al., 2013).

claim: Local ATP synthesis is facilitated via the Ca2+ uptake by mitochondria.
source: Although reports have shown the requirement of local ATP synthesis and provision during sustained synaptic activity (Rangaraju et al., 2014; Sun et al., 2013), which is facilitated via the Ca2+ uptake by mitochondria (Ashrafi et al., 2020), the diffusion of ATP from mitochondria rich regions to boutons devoid of mitochondria may be sufficient to sustain the energetic requirements of synapses (Pathak et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Ashrafi et al., 2020).

claim: The diffusion of ATP from mitochondria rich regions to boutons devoid of mitochondria may be sufficient to sustain the energetic requirements of synapses.
source: Although reports have shown the requirement of local ATP synthesis and provision during sustained synaptic activity (Rangaraju et al., 2014; Sun et al., 2013), which is facilitated via the Ca2+ uptake by mitochondria (Ashrafi et al., 2020), the diffusion of ATP from mitochondria rich regions to boutons devoid of mitochondria may be sufficient to sustain the energetic requirements of synapses (Pathak et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Pathak et al., 2015).

claim: Activity-driven glycolysis via glucose transporter mobilization at presynaptic terminals may provide the necessary energy to sustain PV+ interneuron mediated inhibition during synaptic release.
source: Moreover, the activity-driven glycolysis via glucose transporter mobilization at presynaptic terminals (Ashrafi et al., 2017) may also provide the necessary energy to sustain PV+ interneuron mediated inhibition during synaptic release.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Ashrafi et al., 2017).

claim: Changes in PV+ interneuron excitability and network activity have been associated with alterations in behavior and emergence of neurological and neuropsychiatric disorders.
source: Changes in PV+ interneuron excitability and network activity have been associated with alterations in behavior and emergence of neurological and neuropsychiatric disorders (Inan et al., 2016; Marín, 2012; Pelkey et al., 2017; Zou et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Inan et al., 2016; Marín, 2012; Pelkey et al., 2017; Zou et al., 2016).

claim: The selective loss of Miro1 from PV+ interneurons results in changes in mitochondrial dynamics, axonal remodeling, and network activity that might give rise to anxiety related phenotypes, affecting the behavior of these animals.
source: In conclusion, the selective loss of Miro1 from PV+ interneurons results in changes in mitochondrial dynamics, axonal remodeling, and network activity that might give rise to anxiety related phenotypes, affecting the behavior of these animals.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined observations of mitochondrial, morphological, network, and behavioral changes.

claim: Miro1-dependent mitochondrial positioning is implicated in shaping hippocampal network activity and animal behavior.
source: Our data suggest that Miro1-dependent mitochondrial positioning is implicated in shaping hippocampal network activity and animal behavior.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined observations of network and behavioral changes in Miro1 KO animals.

claim: Miro1-dependent mitochondrial positioning is essential for correct PV+ interneuron function, network activity, and anxiolytic animal behavior.
source: Thus, we show that Miro1-dependent mitochondrial positioning is essential for correct PV+ interneuron function, network activity, and anxiolytic animal behavior.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined observations of mitochondrial, network, and behavioral changes in Miro1 KO animals.
